title: Count Words Opening With a Prefix
statement:
You get a list of lowercase words and a lowercase string pref. Count how many words begin with pref, meaning their first pref.length characters are exactly pref.

A word that equals pref counts. Duplicate words are counted each time they appear.

examples.why: "card" and "cart" start with "car". "scar" contains it but not at the start, and "ca" is too short.
"apple" equals the prefix, which counts. "app" is a prefix of pref, not the other way round.

constraints: All strings contain only lowercase English letters
hints: A word qualifies only if the match is at position 0. Searching anywhere in the word is the classic mistake.
If a word is shorter than pref it cannot qualify.
Compare the first pref.length characters of each word with pref, character by character or with a built-in startsWith.

explain.intuition:
This is a direct scan. For each word, the only question is whether its first m = pref.length characters spell pref. A word shorter than m fails immediately, and the comparison can stop at the first mismatch.

Think of an autocomplete box filtering a short list: with only a hundred words, a plain scan is the right tool. A trie only pays off when you query many prefixes against the same large word list.
steps: For each word, skip it if it is shorter than pref.
Otherwise compare word[i] with pref[i] for i from 0 to m − 1, stopping at the first difference.
If all characters matched, increment count. Return it at the end.
pitfalls: Checking it backwards, i.e. whether the word is a prefix of pref. Then "app" would wrongly count for "apple".

solutions.title: Built-in startsWith
solutions.idea: Count the words for which startsWith(pref) is true.

solutions.title: Manual character comparison
solutions.idea: Skip words shorter than pref; otherwise compare the leading characters one by one and stop at the first mismatch.

followups: You get one word list and a million different prefixes to count. What structure answers each query in O(prefix length)?
Count the words that end with a given suffix instead. Can the same structure help?
